statusDefinitions.source-tested: Implementation and named tests are present in the owning repository. This catalog does not imply those tests were executed in this page build.
statusDefinitions.pages-build: Included in this Learning Center Pages build; automated adapter tests exist, but real browser/device behavior may remain unverified.
statusDefinitions.documented: The responsibility and boundary are documented; an end-to-end integration is not claimed.
statusDefinitions.proposed: A future capability or integration hypothesis. No implementation claim is made.

capabilities.title: Stateful behavior and deterministic updates
capabilities.meaning: Represent behavior as explicit states, transitions, contexts, and processing groups. The host advances work; the state-machine library owns transition semantics.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree contains the runtime and focused update, lifecycle, and integer-backed contract tests. This catalog links the evidence; it does not claim a fresh package release.
capabilities.example: The Learning Center's FSM_API lab lets a learner change inputs, advance a processing group, and inspect resulting state transitions.
capabilities.boundary: FSM_API does not own the UI renderer, the host's scheduling policy, or the semantic interpretation of user input.

capabilities.title: Semantic user intent
capabilities.meaning: Translate an interaction into an explicit, typed intent with context and evidence instead of letting a UI control directly exercise application authority.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree contains SemanticIntent and SemanticInteraction contract tests plus a runnable SemanticIntent host sample.
capabilities.example: Inspect the minimal host sample and follow an intent from its semantic payload into application-owned handling.
capabilities.boundary: An intent describes what was requested; it is not proof of permission, successful execution, or durable user identity.

capabilities.title: Compose a runtime from declared capabilities
capabilities.meaning: Resolve a host-supplied manifest and catalog into a dependency-ordered RuntimeAssembly, with explicit validation and composition outcomes.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree contains the FSM_COS runtime implementation, manifest planning tests, resolved-runtime tests, and a minimal consumer sample.
capabilities.example: Start with the minimal consumer sample, then compare its manifest with the runtime planning and failure-boundary documentation.
capabilities.boundary: FSM_COS composes and returns a runtime assembly. The host owns post-handoff execution and presentation.

capabilities.title: Build a semantic GUI scene
capabilities.meaning: Describe interface structure as a semantic scene model, independently of the platform adapter that eventually presents it.
capabilities.evidence: GUI.Core has a concrete GuiBuilder model and focused Core.Tests coverage. Separate Blazor, WPF, and SVG adapters have their own test projects.
capabilities.example: The FSM-driven bounded oscillator recipe builds a semantic GUI scene from the resulting FSM context.
capabilities.boundary: The semantic model does not itself create a native window, run a browser event loop, or render pixels.

capabilities.title: Serialize a semantic scene as SVG
capabilities.meaning: Translate GUI semantic nodes into an SVG document that can be inspected, embedded, or rendered by an SVG-capable viewer.
capabilities.evidence: SvgGuiRenderer and SVG renderer tests are present in the development tree. The renderer produces a document snapshot; it is not a simulation clock.
capabilities.example: Browse the GUI demonstrations and compare the authored SVG with the semantic scene that generated it.
capabilities.boundary: SVG output is a representation. It does not advance FSM state or claim a live GPU scene.

capabilities.title: Resolve visualizer frames and GPU workloads
capabilities.meaning: Resolve submitted visualizer frames into validated draw work and resource plans, keeping scene data, resource lifetime, and backend execution boundaries explicit.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree contains frame resolution, resource planning, workload encoding, and focused tests for those contracts. Backend and browser support must still be evaluated per host.
capabilities.example: The SoldierField and ArrayFirstWorkload samples expose measurable workloads and browser runner experiments.
capabilities.boundary: A passing resolver test is not proof that every browser exposes WebGPU or that a target device can sustain a given workload.

capabilities.title: Define application-owned protocol meaning
capabilities.meaning: Give events, values, and payloads explicit identities and versioned contracts so producers and consumers can agree on meaning without relying on model-generated interpretation.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree includes protocol definition, event envelope, payload, resolution, and portable fixture conformance tests.
capabilities.example: Use the ProtocolAi quick start or playground to inspect a small protocol exchange.
capabilities.boundary: ProtocolAi defines application-owned contracts. It is not an inference engine or a provider transport.

capabilities.title: Validate structured language
capabilities.meaning: Represent grammar definitions and structured productions so syntax can be parsed and validated against an explicit grammar profile.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree includes grammar definitions, grammar structures, JSON/XML/URI examples, and focused grammar tests.
capabilities.example: Start with the GrammarAi quick start and inspect the JSON or C# grammar test cases.
capabilities.boundary: Grammar validity is not the same as semantic correctness, authorization, or safe execution.

capabilities.title: Turn proposals into governed commands
capabilities.meaning: Model command proposals, arguments, preconditions, and outcomes as explicit contracts so a host can validate a proposed action before execution.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree includes command proposal and instruction models, text codecs, exchange contracts, and atomic-command tests.
capabilities.example: The quick-start sample shows command construction; the MicroBundle quick start explores capability packaging.
capabilities.boundary: A command proposal is not authority to execute. The host remains responsible for approval and effects.

capabilities.title: Evaluate CI evidence and release gates
capabilities.meaning: Collect workflow/build evidence, validate required artifacts, and evaluate dependency and consumer gates as explicit policy decisions.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree contains CI pipeline, workflow evidence, artifact verification, consumer verification, and dependency release-gate contracts with contract tests.
capabilities.example: Inspect the CI evidence sample and the repository's documented workflow/evidence boundaries.
capabilities.boundary: Implemented evidence and gate contracts do not by themselves prove that a fully autonomous cross-repository change→build→assess→apply loop is operational.

capabilities.title: Describe an Experience independently of its host
capabilities.meaning: Define an Experience manifest and resolve its declared semantic requirements separately from the host that chooses how to present it.
capabilities.evidence: The development tree contains manifest contracts and resolver code, along with multiple host/sample projects. The map does not imply every sample is deployable or integrated with every host.
capabilities.example: Read the Experience manifest contract and compare it with the Castle Siege or Capsule Clinic samples.
capabilities.boundary: An authored manifest and a sample host do not establish a universal production host or a complete cross-host lifecycle.

capabilities.title: First-person campus and browser WebGPU proof
capabilities.meaning: Present a source-backed campus catalog in a first-person browser experience and submit VisualizerFrames to a browser WebGPU backend.
capabilities.statusLabel: Pages build + adapter tests; device check pending
capabilities.evidence: The Pages workflow generates city/campus catalog assets, runs CampusWebGpuBackend tests, publishes the Blazor showcase, and deploys on an authorized development workflow dispatch. The README explicitly keeps supportsInstancing disabled until real browser/device validation.
capabilities.example: Open the campus on desktop or mobile. The current tree proof uses eighteen instances of one reusable tree mesh; hardware support is still a separate validation step.
capabilities.boundary: A successful Pages build and adapter unit tests do not prove browser/device WebGPU support, visual correctness, or sustained performance.

capabilities.title: End-to-end autonomous development loop
capabilities.meaning: A governed pipeline that receives a change, builds exact commits, gathers evidence, evaluates policy, and proposes or applies the next change under explicit authority boundaries.
capabilities.evidence: Individual evidence, artifact, and gate contracts exist. This catalog deliberately does not label the complete cross-repository loop operational until a repeatable exact-commit demonstration proves the entire lifecycle.
capabilities.example: The first acceptance demonstration should show one controlled repository change moving through build, evidence collection, assessment, and a separately authorized application step.
capabilities.boundary: A green build, a package artifact, or a passing gate test is not permission to merge, publish, deploy, or mutate another repository.
